Why Slow Reading Wins

Reading slowly is a choice that pays back in attention. The first paragraph sets the pace and tells the reader what kind of time this piece will ask of them, which is more than most pages admit up front.

Most pages are designed to be skimmed, and most readers oblige. A rack with ten slots and a week on the clock changes the arithmetic: every article saved is a promise, and promises are easier to keep when they are few.

The second half of the essay walks through three habits. First, read the whole thing or let it go. Second, write one line about what you took from it. Third, notice how often you save things you never meant to read, and stop saving those.

None of this is new. Commonplace books did the same job for centuries, and the takeaway line is a commonplace entry with a date on it. What is new is the deadline, which is the only part that works without willpower.

A closing note on tools: the best ones are quiet. They should hold what you give them, remind you gently, and get out of the way. Anything that counts, scores or congratulates is working for itself rather than for the reader.

So the practice is simple. Save less. Read what you saved. Keep one sentence. Let the rest compost, which is where the name comes from, and where most of what we save was always going to end up anyway.

If you got this far you read about three hundred words, which at a calm pace is a minute or two, which is about what this test needs to produce a reading-time estimate above the threshold.
